item.title: DeFi Options & Derivatives in 2024–2025: Trends and Key Platforms
item.dc:creator: Andrey Belyakov
item.content:encoded:
Derivatives are back and evolving fast

Decentralized Finance (DeFi) derivatives are making a comeback. After a rocky 2022–2023, on-chain options and futures trading have rebounded with new innovations, better user experiences, and renewed interest. This article explores the latest trends in DeFi options and derivatives as of 2024–2025 and provides an overview of major platforms for asset management and decentralized derivatives trading. We’ll look at structured asset management protocols (like Yearn, Set, Enzyme) as well as derivatives exchanges (from perpetuals on dYdX, Hyperliquid, Lighter and GMX to options on Lyra, Dopex, Opium, and more). Along the way, we’ll highlight how options AMMs, structured products, volatility markets, and cross-chain tech are shaping the DeFi landscape.

Introduction: A Resurgence in DeFi Derivatives

DeFi’s derivatives sector is experiencing a renaissance. After the initial DeFi boom, interest in on-chain options had cooled — by late 2022 and 2023, trading volumes for decentralized options had plummeted. But 2024 brought a dramatic turnaround. On-chain options trading volume surged over 10x year-on-year: September 2024 saw $866 million in nominal volume, up from just $78 million in September 2023. Premiums (the fees paid for options) roughly tripled in that time,​ indicating traders were finally paying for value rather than only scooping up ultra-cheap speculative bets. This surge points to growing demand and confidence in DeFi options markets. See more details here… Perpetual futures DEXs still dominate on-chain derivatives, but the gap is narrowing — in 2023, perp volumes were 400 times larger than options, shrinking to ~160x by late 2024 as options activity picked up. In short, DeFi derivatives are back, and they’re evolving fast.

In short, DeFi derivatives are back, and they’re evolving fast.

Several factors underpin this resurgence. New platforms and products launched, often with incentive programs (like “points mining” rewards) to bootstrap liquidity. For example, the Opyn team’s AEVO exchange attracted billions in monthly volume by offering reward points to active traders, hitting $16B in March 2024 (albeit mostly from dirt-cheap out-of-the-money options)​. Across the board, user experience improved — trading interfaces became friendlier and transaction costs dropped thanks to Layer-2 networks and app-specific chains. And as crypto markets in general picked up in 2024, more users sought on-chain leverage and hedging, fueling growth in both perpetual futures and options. Before diving into the specific trends in options, let’s set the stage with the key platforms that make up today’s DeFi asset management and derivatives ecosystem.

Structured Asset Management Protocols (Yearn, Set, Enzyme, etc.)

One pillar of DeFi is automated asset management — protocols that help users maximize yield or manage portfolios without needing constant manual action. These platforms offer “set-and-forget” strategies, from simple yield farming to complex structured products. Three of the most notable are Yearn Finance, Set Protocol (Index Coop), and Enzyme Finance:

  • Yearn Finance (YFI) — A pioneer of yield aggregation, Yearn pools user deposits into vaults that automatically deploy capital into the best-yielding opportunities in DeFi. Yearn’s strategies handle the heavy lifting of yield farming, compounding returns for users. At its peak in 2021, Yearn managed billions in assets. The bear market shrank those numbers, but Yearn remains a top DeFi yield optimizer with around $200 million in total value locked as of early 2025. It continues to update its vault strategies (the latest Yearn v3 vaults offer more flexible, modular yield strategies on Ethereum and beyond, ​see more). Yearn has also partnered with other DeFi protocols (Curve, Aave, liquid staking providers, etc.) to sustain its yield offerings. Competition is fierce — Convex Finance overtook Yearn in the battle for Curve staking yields see more — but Yearn’s long track record and security focus keep it as a cornerstone for passive crypto investing.
  • Set Protocol / Index Coop — Set Protocol allows the creation of on-chain index funds and strategy baskets. The community-driven Index Coop built on Set’s infrastructure to launch tokens like DeFi Pulse Index (DPI), which bundles top DeFi assets, and other themed index funds. They also offer leveraged index tokens (e.g. 2x leverage ETH or inverse tokens) that rebalance automatically. Index Coop’s products attracted significant AUM during DeFi’s height (DPI once held over $100M+ in assets) and while those numbers dipped in the bear market, the Coop has been innovating. In 2024 they launched improved leveraged tokens on Arbitrum and Base L2s to reduce costs​, see indexcoop.com, introduced new yield-bearing products like hyETH (hybrid ETH staking yield) which saw millions in inflows, and revamped their app UI. These index products make crypto investing more like buying an ETF — diversified and automated. Though a niche in overall DeFi, structured index tokens provide value for users who want broad exposure or automated trading strategies without actively managing a portfolio
  • Enzyme Finance (MLN) — Formerly known as Melon, Enzyme is an on-chain asset management platform where individuals or institutions can create and run their own vaults (essentially decentralized hedge funds). Vault managers can deploy various strategies — trading assets, lending, yield farming — and others can invest in these vaults transparently. Enzyme’s growth has been noteworthy; the protocol hit a new all-time high of $253 million in assets under management in Q1 2024 ​see details. That’s up from a low of ~$35M during the bear market, showing a strong resurgence. Enzyme vaults saw ~$104M in trading volume in that quarter, and new use cases emerged: for example, projects like Diva and Swell used Enzyme to manage liquidity for their liquid staking tokens​ medium.com, and even insurance protocol Nexus Mutual uses Enzyme vaults to earn yield on reserves​. This highlights Enzyme’s flexibility — it’s not just for “DeFi DJNs” running risky funds; it’s also a tool for treasury management and automated strategy execution. As Enzyme continues to integrate with more DeFi protocols (DEXs, lending platforms, etc.), it cements itself as the largest on-chain active asset management platform by TVL according to ​messari.io.

Other honorable mentions in DeFi asset management include Velvet Capital (which offers cross-chain yield farming portfolios), Spool DAO (a yield aggregator focusing on custom risk tranching), and various DAO-focused treasury management tools. But Yearn, Set/IndexCoop, and Enzyme stand out as established leaders enabling users to passively grow their assets or follow active strategies in a non-custodial way. They form the foundation for many structured products in DeFi — including some option-selling vaults that overlap with our next topic.

Decentralized Derivatives Trading Platforms (Perpetuals & Options)

On the trading side of DeFi, derivatives exchanges allow users to go beyond spot trading into futures, perpetuals, and options — all on-chain. By 2024, decentralized derivatives volumes have soared, making up a growing slice of crypto trading. Derivatives DEXs grew from under 3% to about 4% of total DEX volume in 2024, reflecting renewed on-chain speculation​according to tradedog.io​tradedog.io. Let’s overview the major platforms:

Perpetuals

  • Hyperliquid is a decentralized exchange (DEX) built to provide high-performance trading of perpetual contracts. Launched in June 2023, the platform operates on its proprietary HyperEVM, leveraging a custom-built HyperBFT consensus to ensure ultra-low latency and high throughput, which is critical for perpetual trading. By early 2025, Hyperliquid has established itself as a market leader, with over 420,000 active users and a cumulative trading volume exceeding $1.27 trillion. The platform has grown rapidly, capturing 71% of the market share in decentralized derivatives, while its native token, HYPE, now has a market capitalization of over $5.17 billion. Hyperliquid’s market dominance can be seen in its $6.27 billion in daily trading volume and $3.1 billion in open interest, which now rivals industry giants like Deribit and Binance in terms of liquidity. Unlike traditional perpetual exchanges, Hyperliquid operates a fully transparent order book on-chain, offering a decentralized alternative to centralized exchanges (CEXs). The protocol supports up to 50× leverage and aims to disrupt the industry by offering zero gas fees and instant trade execution. With an expanding ecosystem of Layer-2 networks, Hyperliquid is also working to introduce more advanced features, like multi-collateral and cross-chain trading, setting it up as one of the dominant platforms in DeFi’s perpetuals space.
  • dYdX — The most prominent decentralized perpetuals exchange. dYdX offers perpetual futures (similar to futures contracts without expiry) for a wide range of assets with up to 20× leverage. In 2021–22, dYdX on Ethereum L2 (StarkWare) famously at times surpassed Coinbase’s volume, fueled by liquidity mining incentives. It has since transitioned those incentives and is now evolving further: in late 2023, dYdX launched its own app-specific blockchain (built on Cosmos SDK) to maximize throughput and control its orderbook environment. In 2024, dYdX facilitated over $270 billion in trading volume, see more ​decrypt.co, pushing its cumulative volume since 2021 above $1.4 trillion — a testament to how much usage it has garnered. This was aided by a “Trade Anything” expansion: dYdX’s V4 allowed listing many new markets instantly, reaching 175 markets by early 2025 and introducing a MegaVault with $79M TVL to deepen liquidity. One out of every three dollars traded on all perp DEXes in 2023 could be attributed to dYdX’s 2024 volumes, underscoring its dominance. With a full order book, advanced trading features, and the performance of a dedicated chain, dYdX aims to rival centralized exchanges — yet it remains non-custodial and governed by DYDX token holders. The platform’s trajectory into 2025 is focused on that “trade anything” vision: even more markets (potentially including stocks or commodities as synthetics) and an improved, fully decentralized order matching engine.
  • Lighter is a cutting-edge decentralized platform focused on perpetual contract trading with a strong emphasis on scalability, security, and transparency. Leveraging zk-rollup technology, Lighter processes large volumes of trades with minimal latency, enabling high-speed transactions and ensuring low-cost operations. The platform’s unique approach to decentralized trading is based on zkLighter, a zk-rollup layer built on Ethereum, designed to handle tens of thousands of transactions per second. This layer helps Lighter achieve sub-5-millisecond latency for its trades, offering professional traders and institutions a robust and seamless trading experience. Since its launch in 2022, Lighter has grown steadily, expanding its user base through strategic partnerships with networks like Arbitrum and zkSync, and introducing advanced zero-knowledge cryptography to enhance transparency and trust in its order book. As of 2024, Lighter is focused on offering perpetual contracts with minimal fees, making it a competitive option for professional users who need low-latency execution. While trading volume statistics have been gradually rising, Lighter’s appeal lies in its zk-powered scalability and its ability to combine Ethereum’s security with faster, more efficient transaction processing, making it an attractive platform for institutional DeFi traders seeking speed and security in the decentralized market.
  • GMX — If dYdX is the orderbook king, GMX represents the AMM approach to perpetuals. Launched on Arbitrum (and later Avalanche), GMX lets users trade BTC, ETH and other majors with up to 50x leverage against a pooled liquidity model. Liquidity providers contribute assets into a basket called GLP, which acts as the counterparty to trades (essentially, LPs are the “house” taking the other side of longs/shorts). GMX became immensely popular in 2022–2023 for its simplicity and strong fee share to stakers. By early 2025, GMX had amassed about $600 million TVL across its pools, see ​coinbureau.com, and facilitated over $140 billion in total trading volume to date​, see stats.gmx.io. Daily volumes often range in the hundreds of millions of dollars. The protocol’s success meant GLP liquidity providers collectively earned tens of millions in fees (annualized fees were around $60M as of late 2024) according to ​defillama.com. In 2024, GMX v2 launched with improvements: more asset markets (including “synthetic” markets for assets not fully collateralized by the pool), adjustable leverage based on open interest, and features like limit orders​ more details​. GMX’s rise demonstrated demand for user-friendly, low-slippage on-chain leverage — traders enjoy zero price impact execution (pegged to oracle pricing), and LPs earn yield though they must manage exposure risks. GMX’s model has inspired similar protocols (e.g. Gains Network on Polygon/Arbitrum using synthetic assets, Perpetual Protocol v2 with a virtual AMM model, etc.), but GMX remains the flagship for AMM-based perp trading.
  • Synthetix & Perp Aggregators — Another pillar in DeFi derivatives is Synthetix, which was a pioneer in on-chain synthetic assets. Synthetix originally let users mint “synth” tokens tracking assets like gold, stocks, or indices, but in 2022–2023 it refocused on perpetual futures too. Synthetix’s liquidity (coming from SNX stakers who collateralize the system) powers several front-end exchanges like Kwenta, Decentralized BitMex (dBMEX), and others on Optimism. By mid-2024 Synthetix facilitated billions in monthly perp volume, although its approach (pooled debt backing all trades) competes with GMX’s model. Additionally, aggregators emerged: platforms that route trades to the best available derivative venue. For example, Polynomial on Optimism initially built options vaults but later pivoted to a “derivatives L2” and perp aggregator​. Hyperliquid, a newer player, even built a specialized Layer-1 chain for ultra-fast perp trading and reportedly airdropped $1.8B in tokens to users​ (see tradedog.io) — signaling the lengths new derivatives projects go to bootstrap liquidity. The result of all this competition? By 2024, decentralized perpetual exchanges handled ~$1.5 trillion in volume, more than double the prior year according to ​decrypt.co, and are on track to challenge centralized platforms in liquidity. A growing array of choices (orderbooks vs AMMs, multi-chain options, incentive wars) is driving rapid innovation in on-chain futures.

Option protocols

Unlike perpetuals, which saw a clear formula for success, DeFi options trading has been more fragmented. Multiple protocols with different designs have vied to bring options (calls, puts, exotic options) on-chain. Here are the major ones:

  • Opyn/Aevo — Opyn was an early DeFi options protocol (back in 2020 it introduced oTokens for ETH puts/calls). However, Opyn struggled to find a profitable model purely on-chain and did not generate revenue from its v2 options system. In 2023 the Opyn team shifted focus to launching Aevo, a semi-decentralized options exchange with an off-chain orderbook but on-chain settlement. Aevo went live with an aggressive incentives program; as noted, it achieved record volumes (over $2B in April 2024 after an astounding $16B in March during a promo burst)​. While much of that volume was likely miners farming points via low-cost trades, Aevo demonstrated that liquidity can exist for on-chain options given the right infrastructure. Opyn’s pivot to Aevo (and even developing perp contracts) means the original Opyn protocol has taken a backseat, but their legacy lives on in many current projects (the oToken standard influenced later designs).
  • Lyra (now Derive) — Lyra is a decentralized options AMM that launched on Optimism in 2021. It uses a pooled liquidity model (somewhat akin to an AMM, with dynamic volatility curves) to let users buy or sell options on ETH, BTC, etc. Lyra showed promise but faced challenges with liquidity and capital efficiency on L2. In 2024, Lyra undertook a major transformation: it rebranded to Derive and launched its own appchain on the Optimism Stack (Derive Chain), shifting to a hybrid orderbook model, see ​binance.com. This move aimed to combine the best of both worlds — the performance of an orderbook exchange with on-chain settlement/finality. The result: Derive now regularly clears $200–300 million in monthly options volume, a substantial amount for a DeFi options platform. By leveraging an application-specific chain, Derive can offer a smoother trading experience (competitive with centralized platforms) while still being non-custodial. Lyra’s journey exemplifies the evolution of options AMMs: starting simple, then embracing more sophisticated designs (and even custom blockchains) to improve efficiency.
  • Dopex (rebranded to Stryke) — Dopex (Decentralized Options Exchange) made waves in 2021–2022 with its novel products like single staking options vaults (SSOVs) and Atlantic options (options with depositable collateral that could be used to earn yield until exercise). However, Dopex’s initial model, which relied on liquidity pools for each strike and expiration, struggled with utilization and liquidity fragmentation. In the past year, Dopex underwent a makeover: it rebranded to Stryke and introduced a concentrated liquidity AMM (CLAMM) for options, similar in spirit to Uniswap v3 but for option markets. This change dramatically improved capital efficiency and reignited usage — Stryke’s monthly trading volumes climbed into the $20–50 million range over the past year​. Along with the AMM upgrade, Stryke simplified its token economics by phasing out its rebate token rDPX and consolidating value into a single SYK token (with xSYK for stakers)​. This streamlining helped restore community confidence. Dopex/Stryke’s resurgence underscores how protocols can “turn the tide” by pivoting designs — in this case, moving from a clunky dual token + inefficient pools to a cleaner model. It remains one of the go-to venues for on-chain options on Arbitrum, supporting many option strategies with decent liquidity after the revamp.
  • Opium (rebranded to Zero Options)— Opium Protocol is a DeFi derivatives platform known for creativity: it has offered anything from credit default swaps on MakerDAO to insurance on DeFi exploits. As the options trend picked up, Opium pivoted toward intent based architecture and includes ultra-short-term options. By 2024 Opium’s focus is on new version of protocol that is intent based, and essentially intraday options akin to the 0DTE craze in traditional markets. This aligns with the growing retail appetite for quick, leveraged bets and need to hedge short term operations between chains and layers. Opium’s approach often involves a request-for-quote mechanism and customizable payoffs. While not the largest player by volume, Opium provides infrastructure for exotic derivatives and has carved a niche serving advanced traders who want things like same-day expiring options or bespoke hedging instruments. Its shift to 0DTE also mirrors a broader volatility market trend: many traders prefer short-dated options for speculative plays, and protocols are adapting to facilitate that safely on-chain.
  • Others — The DeFi options space is crowded with innovators. Hegic, one of the earliest options AMMs, introduced 0DTE options in summer 2024 to ride the short-term volatility wave. Premia launched a v3 with a hybrid model (part AMM, part on-chain orderbook) on Arbitrum, doing $6–15M monthly volume and working on a v4 that will improve collateral efficiency and even add perp trading. Rysk emerged with an innovative vaults-as-market-maker design — its upcoming V2 creates vaults that algorithmically provide liquidity to decentralized orderbook. Thales focused on binary options (yes/no bets on price moves) and averaged a modest $5M/month (though late 2024 saw a dip to ~$1M)​. On the more exotic side, protocols like Umoja synthesize options through dynamic hedging with spot and perps, and Volmex introduced volatility index tokens (like an on-chain VIX for ETH). It’s a rich ecosystem, though not all have survived — e.g. PsyOptions (a Solana options protocol) shut down its vaults by mid-2024, and others like Ribbon Finance shifted focus away from options (Ribbon’s team is now more focused on Aevo exchange, though Ribbon’s structured option vaults still operate with much lower TVL)​.

In summary, the major derivatives platforms in DeFi span a spectrum: from perpetuals exchanges (dYdX, GMX, Synthetix) that handle huge volumes of continuous futures, to options platforms (Lyra/Derive, Dopex/Stryke, Opyn/Aevo, Opium) experimenting with different market mechanisms. Each contributes to making DeFi a more complete trading ecosystem. Next, let’s zoom in on the key trends shaping these options and derivatives markets in 2024–2025.

Key Trends in DeFi Options & Derivatives (2024–2025)

1. Options AMMs 2.0 and the Growth of On-Chain Options: Early attempts at on-chain options (like simplistic automated market makers in 2020–21) often suffered from poor liquidity and high risk for liquidity providers. The past year has seen major improvements in options AMMs. Protocols adopted concentrated liquidity and hybrid models, leading to better pricing and lower slippage. Dopex’s switch to CLAMM and Premia’s hybrid orderbook/AMM are prime examples, each boosting volumes and utilization​. Meanwhile, purely orderbook-based DEXs for options also went live (Aevo, Deribit-like experiences on-chain). The net effect is that users actually have viable venues to trade options decentralizally, whereas a year ago liquidity was so sparse that most stuck to centralized options or avoided them entirely. The 10x jump in on-chain options volume by late 2024​ demonstrates this new viability. We’re likely at the start of an upswing for DeFi options, as better AMMs/orderbooks attract more market makers, which in turn attracts more traders — a virtuous cycle.

2. Structured Products and Yield Strategies Involving Options: Structured products were once the darling of DeFi — in 2021, protocols like Ribbon Finance soared in TVL by offering covered-call vaults and put-selling strategies that generated yield. By 2023, many of those saw declines or even shuttered (by late 2024, 9 out of 13 options vault protocols had wound down or pivoted away). The tide is turning here as well. The structured products that survived are adapting: Ribbon remains operational (though smaller, and its team is off building Aevo); Cega introduced exotic options like knock-in/knock-out notes and even integrated yield tokens from Pendle for extra returns​; Thetanuts likewise launched vaults leveraging Pendle’s yield-bearing tokens​. In short, structured options products are finding a second wind by integrating with yield sources like liquid staking yields or Pendle yield tokens to make their payouts more attractive. New projects (e.g. 3Jane, a Ribbon fork, or Superhedge, which combines yield farming on Aave/Pendle with buying options for downside protection​) are reimagining what on-chain structured products can do. These offer users accessible strategies: for instance, deposit ETH and let the vault automatically sell calls every week for yield, or deposit stablecoins and let the vault buy protective puts funded by yield farming interest. Such products abstract the complexities of options into a simple deposit-and-earn format. After a hype cycle and a cooldown, structured options are re-emerging as sustainable yield solutions, particularly as crypto volatility creeps up (making options premiums richer). Some structured products have expanded cross-chain (Ribbon on multiple chains, Cega beyond Solana to EVM, etc.), tapping into wider liquidity.

3. Rise of 0DTE and Short-Term Options: If one trend encapsulates 2023–2024 in both TradFi and DeFi options, it’s the explosion of zero-day-to-expiry (0DTE) options. In traditional markets, 0DTE S&P 500 options grew to ~50% of options volume by 2023 as thrill-seeking traders flooded in​. DeFi is following suit. Protocols like Opium and Hegic now offer same-day expiring options, and retail traders are using them to bet on intraday moves with leverage. The attraction is clear: 0DTE options are cheap (because they are very short-lived) yet can provide outsized gains if the underlying makes a sharp move in hours. On-chain, 0DTEs also avoid long waiting periods or liquidity lock-ups. However, they’re risky and tricky to price. To accommodate, DeFi platforms had to refine their tech — updating pricing models more frequently, automating exercise/settlement to the minute, etc. The push for 0DTE is part of a broader category of “volatility markets”: products that let users play pure volatility. For instance, some platforms offer options on volatility indices or combinations of options (straddles/strangles) packaged for betting on volatility itself. We’re even seeing on-chain funds focused solely on 0DTE strategies. While still a small niche, the presence of 0DTE options in DeFi shows that decentralized markets are mature enough to handle fast-paced, high-risk products that were once the domain of professional trading firms. It’s a sign of growing sophistication.

4. On-Chain Liquidity Innovations (App Chains and Unified Liquidity): As mentioned earlier, one big trend is platforms deploying their own chains or specialized environments. dYdX’s appchain and Lyra/Derive’s OP Chain are two examples where trading infrastructure is moving to sovereign chains for speed and customization. This raises an interesting question for “DeFi purity” — some argue these app chains sacrifice a bit of decentralization (since they often have a limited validator set or rely on cross-chain bridges) in exchange for performance​. But users have shown they value a CEX-like experience as long as custody remains decentralized. Another innovation is unified liquidity across markets. GMX’s single GLP pool model inspired others; now protocols like Unified MM and even Synthetix’s upcoming V3 talk about one liquidity pool backing many derivatives. This can make markets more capital-efficient (no need to fragment liquidity by each trading pair or expiry). There’s also exploration of intent-based and RFQ systems: e.g. Arrow Markets on Avalanche uses RFQ for options quotes​, and Predy is working on intent-based options trading​ where a user’s intent to trade is matched optimally via off-chain agents. All these efforts aim to solve the hardest problem in DeFi derivatives: liquidity. By improving how liquidity is pooled and accessed (whether through custom chains, better AMMs, or off-chain matchmaking), these innovations are gradually closing the gap between DeFi and TradFi in market quality.

5. User Experience and Accessibility Improvements: A less quantifiable but crucial trend is the vastly improved UX in DeFi derivatives. A few years ago, using a DeFi options dApp was intimidating — clunky interfaces, confusing Greeks, manual rollover of expiring positions, etc. In 2024–2025, we see much more polished products. Many options platforms now offer intuitive dashboards, integrate with popular wallets and portfolio trackers, and provide learning material so users understand strategies. There are also aggregators like tealfinance that compare option prices across protocols to ensure users get the best deal​. We even have DeFi options vaults discoverable in wallet apps, so a user can, say, deposit into a covered call strategy straight from a mobile interface. Moreover, cross-chain UX has improved with better bridging and messaging protocols (e.g. using LayerZero to bridge collateral or settle trades from one chain to another). For example, a user on Polygon might buy an option that’s actually settled by liquidity on Ethereum, without needing to manually move funds — the protocols handle it under the hood. All this reduces friction, making on-chain derivatives less of a geeky niche and more of a mainstream-friendly product. When combined with the transparency and self-custody benefits, DeFi derivatives become an appealing alternative to centralized exchanges, especially for those worried about exchange solvency or looking for unique products not offered elsewhere.

6. Cross-Chain Expansion and Composability: Finally, DeFi derivatives are no longer confined to Ethereum mainnet. Cross-chain expansion is a key trend, both for reaching new users and for leveraging different chains’ strengths. Many protocols are deploying on multiple networks: we have options on Layer 2s (Lyra on Optimism, Dopex on Arbitrum), on alternative L1s (Ribbon and Cega expanded from Ethereum to Avalanche/Solana, Arrow on Avalanche, Zeta started on Solana), and even on emerging chains like Berachain (where IVX is offering 0DTE options). This multi-chain presence means traders can choose the environment with the best fees or speeds for them. It also means composability between ecosystems: e.g. using an option from one protocol as collateral in another protocol on a different chain is becoming plausible. A concrete example is projects like Across and LayerZero enabling something like cross-chain margin — you might post collateral on Ethereum but trade perps on Arbitrum, with the messaging layer keeping it in sync. We’re not fully there yet, but the groundwork is being laid. Ultimately, the vision is a unified cross-chain derivatives market where it doesn’t matter which chain you’re on; you can access any derivative seamlessly. Achieving that will likely be a major focus through 2025.

Conclusion: Outlook for DeFi Derivatives

DeFi is not limited to swaps and loans anymore; it now encompasses a vibrant, growing derivatives market

The period of 2024–2025 is proving to be a turning point for DeFi options and derivatives. We’re seeing the maturing of products and platforms that had early promise but needed refinement. Options protocols have survived a trial by fire and emerged with better designs, while perpetuals platforms continue to innovate and draw serious trading volume (with dYdX and others even forecasting DEX derivatives volumes to reach trillions in coming years​). Perhaps most importantly, user trust is rebuilding. The crypto community watched CeFi platforms falter in 2022, which has driven many to “trust the code” instead of intermediaries. As yields from simple lending have diminished, users are exploring structured vaults and option strategies to boost returns, bringing fresh capital into these protocols.

Of course, challenges remain. Liquidity fragmentation, regulatory scrutiny, smart contract risks, and the perennial user education hurdle all persist. Not every project will thrive — we’ve seen a fair share of pivots (moving from an options AMM to a perp options aggregator) and failures. However, the trajectory is clear: DeFi is not limited to swaps and loans anymore; it now encompasses a vibrant, growing derivatives market. From hedge funds seeking on-chain hedges to traders buying a 0DTE ETH call for fun, the spectrum of participation is widening.

In summary, the latest trends in DeFi derivatives point to a future where any financial instrument can potentially be found in decentralized form — with options and futures leading the charge. The combination of improved protocols (Yearn’s vaults, Set’s indexes, Enzyme’s managed funds) and advanced trading platforms (dYdX, GMX, Lyra, Dopex, and more) is making the DeFi ecosystem more comprehensive than ever. As 2025 unfolds, keep an eye on these platforms and trends: we’re likely to witness even higher volumes, new cross-chain products, and perhaps the holy grail of DeFi options — matching the scale of their perpetual swap cousins. The road to get there will be exciting and undoubtedly bumpy, but one thing is certain: DeFi’s innovative spirit is alive and well in the world of options and derivatives.

LARGE PROTOCOL UPDATE: BUILDING ON THE BEAR MARKET

-Please carefully read the disclaimer below-

2022 Summary:

  • The Opium Protocol has seen a staggering 500 million USD in traded notional in the past year;
  • The highly-anticipated Opium v2 was successfully launched on Arbitrum and Polygon, bringing even more functionality and flexibility for market making and arbitrage;
  • The protocol boasts a custom derivative constructor for altcoin and exotic options or futures, allowing for an unprecedented level of customisation;
  • Decentralised Order Books, built on the cutting-edge 1inch Limit Order Protocol and integrated with 1inch pathfinder, provide unparalleled efficiency and security;
  • The release of RFQ system v1.0 brings support for protocol-agnostic DeFi options, further expanding the possibilities of the protocol;
  • The protocol agnostic Dutch auctions feature, enables both users and third party smart contracts to launch auctions in order to get fair price;
  • The Web3 ID protocol, known as “Know Your Cat” (KYC) was also launched and released, adding an extra layer of security and compliance to the platform.

Looking behind

As we reflect on the past year, we are filled with gratitude for the dedication and passion of our community. From the countless hours spent on calls and chats, to the tireless contributions on Github, you have been the driving force behind our progress and success.

It is with great excitement that we share with you some of the highlights from the past year. We have seen numerous deployments and achieved many milestones that we are proud to share. We hope that you will join us in celebrating these accomplishments and look forward to continued growth and success in the coming year.

The Opium protocol is a part of innovation in the DeFi space, offering a sophisticated settlement protocol for derivatives that is now branching out to include the vital aspect of regulation-friendly infrastructure (RegFi). As the industry matures, it is becoming increasingly clear that all DeFi projects must pay heed to regulatory concerns to reach their full potential. The Opium team, along with its dedicated community and contributors, is taking this challenge head-on by building open infrastructure that makes it simple for other projects to harness the power of the protocol.

The past year has seen the unveiling of the second version of the Opium Protocol, a marvel of engineering that is more efficient, faster, and more cost-effective than ever before. Deployed on the Arbitrum and Polygon blockchains, this iteration of the protocol enables the effortless creation of custom decentralized derivatives. This is a monumental achievement that allows for the launch of Dutch auctions and automated strategies that are updated with the latest v2.0 features. With this update, any smart contract or Dapp can now launch a Dutch auction with the goal of buying or selling specific options, futures, or other tokens via a mechanism that is not only price efficient but also gas efficient. This ensures that any smart contract can now buy or sell specific tokens, such as call options, with the assurance that the price will be fair. This is because, not only are market makers participating in the auction, but 1inch routers and arbitrageurs are also taking part.

The Opium Automatic Strategies have also undergone a dramatic improvement, now supporting custom logic for trading on spot or derivatives crypto markets. Thanks to a better architecture and the use of Gnosis Safe as a core module, they have become incredibly flexible in terms of strategy. Anyone can now deploy and own an Automated Strategy and instantly take advantage of the Opium infrastructure, such as liquidity from market makers and other RegFi ecosystem and custom products that are created on Opium. This is the result of tireless efforts of our team and community, and it is a testament to the power of collaboration and innovation.

Lets dive into details…

Looking Towards RegFi

Decentralized derivatives, despite their potential, have yet to see widespread adoption and demand. Some have attributed this to the prevalence of wash trading on semi-centralized exchanges, farming-driven liquidity, and whales paying fees to protocols in exchange for tokens.

“DeFi and RegFi are not adversaries, they are allies that enhance and support each other in a harmonious union”, Andrey Belyakov

However, as the DeFi space matures, many experts predict that this will change. As the need for options, interest rate swaps, and futures arises from mature ecosystems where individuals and institutions consider not only initial growth but also hedging and taking specific risks, DeFi derivatives are expected to gain traction. This pattern is reminiscent of what happened in the spot market: first, the development of a centralized market, then the emergence of DeFi, enabled by arbitrage — think of Uniswap’s development. We are now at a stage where centralised derivative exchanges are seeing increased adoption, and the system is ready for DeFi equivalents to thrive.

While decentralized finance holds great promise, the traditional financial system still dwarfs it in size and scope. The true potential for growth lies in attracting demand from the traditional side, and we see that institutions are eager to participate. However, they are waiting for clear regulatory frameworks to be put in place. Paradoxically, events such as the collapse of FTX will likely lead to increased regulation for centralized exchanges, which in turn will drive more adoption of DeFi. This is because, for many, DeFi is cheaper, easier, and sometimes even faster than centralized finance, and it is definitely much more transparent and auditable.

The Opium Team is actively working with a few institutional players to develop a transparent and compliant framework for RegFi that will still utilize the Opium Protocol, but in a compliant manner. Stay tuned for more information on this exciting development.

Opium Protocol 2.0

It has been an honor to bring the Opium 2.0 protocol to fruition, following rigorous testing and review by independent auditors. The new version of the protocol boasts a number of exciting features and improvements, including:

  • Unique ID for Long and Short positions, which can be redeemed or minted at any time in a 1:1 proportion with the corresponding collateral;
  • Significantly reduced gas costs;
  • Increased customisation options for products;
  • Enhanced efficiency for arbitrageurs;
  • Gas-less permissions for position holders;
  • More decentralised governance system and flexible oracle design;

The deployment of the new version was done on the Arbitrum mainnet, and the community is already actively building on top of it. Recently Polygon deployment was also done. Migration tools will be likely offered for those who wish to transition from v1.0 to v2.0. However, Opium v1.0 will remain operational as long as Ethereum exists and there are users of it, as it is an immutable set of smart contracts.

For more information, please read the technical article.

Trustless DeFi infrastructure

Opium v2.0 boasts a trustless infrastructure that seamlessly connects different components of the protocol, as well as linking the protocol to other protocols and DeFi “legos.” In addition to the protocol, a suite of features were conceptualized, developed and implemented in the year 2022, such as:

  • a limit order protocol for Opium positions with a distinct trading view;
  • an enhanced version of the Opium position explorer;
  • a Request for Quote (RFQ) system protocol for multi-swaps (all or nothing) and clearing of various positions (protocol agnostic);
  • Dutch auctions that can be launched by both users and smart contracts;
  • API and SDK resources, improved documentation to promote community involvement;
  • and a web3 based Know Your Customer (Know Your Cat) platform that may grants access to users based on their wallets and verifications on other platforms, which was crafted in collaboration with Binance team and utilizing Binance’s own KYC system.

In the realm of DeFi, we firmly believe that the composability of protocols and ecosystems is one of the key advantages and infrastructure trend is one of the most important trends along with RegFi direction.

Introducing ‘Know Your Cat” ID (web3 KYC analogue)

Opium Team is launching KnowYourCat.id, which connects various data sources to create reliable “compliance whitelists.” This allows projects (including the Opium itself) to easily receive information, such as “non-US person,” with a certainty or probability, through both API and on-chain methods. In order to growth and mass adoption, it is important for creating compliant DeFi products. Few projects are currently building on top of the KnowYourCat and will only work with compliant DeFi pools. Projects like RealT.co already announced integrating KnowYourCat technology.

CATegories — converting traits into an access token

Your token, bound to the Cheshire Cat, holds a wealth of information and characteristics, yet it is particularly intriguing how it categorizes you. According to specific rules for each category, you may fall into it if you possess certain traits or a trait combination. For instance, if you possess a verified Know Your Customer proof (one of many) that is only accessible to non-US individuals, you may be placed in the “non-US” category. In this example, the Cat analyses dozens of KYC proofs on the blockchain and assigns you to the appropriate category if even one trait is present. These categories and their rules can be easily created by anyone, allowing projects to establish their own categorization and define the criteria for inclusion.

Once an address has a category, it also holds a Non-Fungible Token (NFT) access token on its balance, you possess such a token only if you meet the qualifications and possess the corresponding set of traits. These access tokens are utilized for logging into decentralized apps, gaining access to smart contracts or private liquidity pools, private environments, protocols and tokens. A prime example is whitelisted DeFi product that is open for anyone who holds one of several trusted KYC verifications. Another example is whitelisted DeFi product or voting for anyone in the “human” category.

The Cat holds great potential, but it is important to note that it is not a conventional KYC and does not serve as a replacement for it in any way. However, it is a fascinating concept for how KYC may evolve in the future. Imagine not having to submit a photo of your passport to untrusted exchanges, where they could potentially sell your data on the black market, but rather presenting a zero-knowledge proof that you are a Dutch citizen. Such a proof confirms that you possess a government digital ID without disclosing any personal information.

We believe in web3 id and that it can bring compliant and convenient tools without lose of privacy.

Dutch Auctions v2.0

It becomes effortless to tap into the bountiful resources of the Opium ecosystem, such as liquidity and Dutch auctions 2.0, which are expertly managed by professional market makers. Dutch auctions v2.0 will provide a more fair and transparent method of obtaining liquidity and they are integrated with 1inch pathfinder. That will ensure that there is a maximum number of liquidity sources that can “participate” in the auction. Together, we are creating a brighter future for the DeFi space.

Automated Strategies 2.0

For nigh on two years now, the Opium community has been designing and implementing automated strategy staking pools, a concept that is both elegant and straightforward. The idea is to allow token holders to stake their assets within the pool and have a pre-programmed strategy, such as the selling of call options on a weekly basis, executed on their behalf. These strategies have proven to be quite successful, in part due to the community’s focus on lower risk profiles compared to their competitors. However, there were calls to improve the architecture and modules of these staking pools to make them even more flexible. As a result, Automated Strategies 2.0 were brought to life, audited, and deployed.

Built on the solid foundation of the Gnosis Safe core and custom Opium modules that manage the safe, these new strategies offer unparalleled flexibility and security. The modules are responsible for executing strategies, accounting, and ensuring safe execution, to name a few. With this architecture, one can design covered call strategies that collect premium in DAI/USDT while keeping the main token balance stable, or the pool can automatically provide liquidity to Uniswap v3 within a desired range for any unused funds. The possibilities are endless within the Opium ecosystem, where custom instruments and market-making auctions are available to those looking to build their own strategies and take advantage of the infrastructure.

Community and developers

The Opium Community continues to flourish and attract the finest financial and technical minds, as well as teams who are tirelessly developing and exploring the possibilities of the protocol. If you seek to be part of a decentralized collective of innovators, create your own DeFi visions and tools, reach out to us through Telegram, Twitter, or our web forum.

It may proof humanity, KYC and region of a holder

You can mint your Cheshir (left bottom icon) or BAB token and participate in this experiment. If you are a holder of BAB your cat will automatically embed this information and change the color.

Intro

Last year the Opium team presented Cheshire cat NFTs that can be used as an access token and also acquire the reputation of the user, KYC, humanity checks, and much more. Those NFTs are only transferable to your other addresses and they provide an interesting basis for the development of decentralized compliance tools, opening new possibilities.

JavaScript is not available.

Even though not every project needs compliance or wants to implement, we are big fans of such developments. It is not only helping to implement necessary checks but also opens DeFi protocols for institutional investors and “pro/arc/regFi” version of protocols. We believe that this will make DeFi stronger and more mature, also leading to institutional adoption.

A few weeks ago, Binance introduced a great new feature — BAB tokens. These soul-bound tokens are used as proof of identity for Binance users who have completed KYC verification.

BAB tokens help Cheshire to implement humanity checks, regional checks, and KYC checks all at the same time. We couldn’t miss out on this great initiative, so we immediately implemented these standards into our Cheshire cats. We’re now ready for development and experimentation on this exciting journey*!

“BAB token will function as a Binance identity that can be used and verified by third-party protocols for a variety of purposes. This will help eradicate familiar issues relating to airdrops and even bots, helping establish a safer and more accountable space”, says Binance blog

If you have a Cheshire cat NFT and also have BAB tokens from Binance, your cat will become now “Binance style” — yellow with black stripes. You will also have access to certain products that other users don’t have. Projects will know that the yellow cat can only belong to someone who has passed the Binance verification. This means that the person is a real human and is not from the US or any other jurisdiction that is prohibited by Binance. Also, different yellow Cheshires cannot represent the same person.

If you have a Cheshire cat NFT and also have BAB tokens from Binance, your cat will become now“Binance style” — yellow with black stripes.

Our team sees it as a large and interesting step towards more sustainable systems and extra possibilities in crypto. The Opium community and a few other teams keep building and experimenting with Cheshire. New updates will follow soon.

BAB tokens

We believe that this initiative of Binance connects compliant CeFi with DeFi in a very simple, elegant, and convenient way. Existing verified users of the exchange without any additional effort can:

  • participate in closed pools and special products/airdrops,
  • get fair governance power and participate in smarter voting,
  • participate in quadratic voting and other game-theory algorithms with increased “human power”,
  • proof that they are not a bots etc;

You can mint your Cheshire or BAB token and participate in this experiment. If you are a holder of BAB your cat will automatically embed this information and change the color.

How Cheshire works

Cheshire cats are minted on Ethereum and they store a snapshot of several qualities in their DNA.

DNA and genes

There are two types of genes in DNA:

  1. unique genes that identify the cat, and
  2. genes that represent “acquired traits”

These acquired traits can be contributed by projects that the cat interacts with. The more you interact with your cat, the more acquired traits your cat may have. For example, if you are a verified user of 1inch, an active voter on AAVE, or a participant of Gitcoin, your cat may acquire this information. Your NFT becomes sort of a “digital passport” where projects can put their crypto-stamps, that correspond to your reputation, verification, achievements, etc.

Each gene can be added to store information from a participating provider or be aggregated from other blockchains via bridges. We worked with projects like Izyum, to bring data from the BNB chain to the Ethereum mainnet via a Merkle three.

Transfers

At first, when Vitalik Buterin introduced SBT idea early this year, initial comments were regarding transferability and we also see a great point of improvement there.

Normally, Soulbound Token (SBT) is not transferable, however, we see a great opportunity to transfer your digital ID/access token to your other wallets. In the current state, both sender and receiver must sign the statement that they are the same owner. However we are discussing different options here, please contact Opium Team to join the brainstorming. For instance, it could be a limited number of transfers with crypto signatures on both sides or delegation, etc.

“A soulbound item, once picked up, cannot be transferred or sold to another player”, says the article of Vitalik. However, we believe, there is no contradiction, as transfers to your own adress are not transfers to another player.

Looking forward

In order to grow and work with institutions, DeFi services need to have compliant instruments. However, due to blockchain limitations, it is not always possible to use old approaches. So, it is super interesting to build these instruments together with protocols.

We are also working on zk-verification so that banks and other financial institutions can provide certain cryptographic proofs on-chain without disclosing sensitive client data.

item.dc:creator: Andrey Belyakov
item.content:encoded:
Selling ETH options on “gas efficient & optimal revenue” auctions

TLDR; Dutch auctions are part of price discovery in Opium 2.0. Non-interactive and extremely cheap, they are ideal for both blockchain and DeFi options.

The Dutch auction is the open descending price counterpart of the English auction. Here the auction has a start value higher than every interested bidder, and gradually lowered until there is a bidder that is interested at that price.

Pricing of DeFi options

The use of DeFi/crypto options is becoming more and more popular. As usual, the initial demand comes from professional players via centralized settlement but we see that first decentralized versions are growing in popularity too — used both by smart contracts as well as end users! Just like Uniswap got popular after centralised exchanges became mature, DeFi protocols may see an increase in adoption when there is enought centralised markets.

Pricing options (and especially crypto-options) is difficult, in the end it is all about the market price that you can get. Market-makers, crypto hedge funds, and other participants are trying to create valuation models or hedge when possible.

When you want to trade such a complex instrument from a smart contract there is almost no other way than using an auction. Many automated trading strategies utilized by Opium, Ribbon, Thetanuts, and other DeFi Option Vaults are running decentralized auctions weekly. However, those auctions can be inefficient on gas, time, and revenue. According to the game theory, a Dutch auction can lead to optimal revenue and can be better than a normal English auction while being non-interactive.

Why “Dutch auction” is the best for DeFi

First of all, the Dutch auction is one of the best revenue optimizing auctions. According to game theory, it leads to the same outcome as other optimal auctions.

Second, it is non-interactive and gas efficient. Taker only needs to send one transaction, picking up the lot at the desired price.

Third, the auction has an executable price from the beginning and will be aggregated by pathfinders like 1inch.io and others. Thousands of traders and hundreds of liquidity sources are “participating” in the auction together with private market makers and arbitrageurs.

Thousands of traders and hundreds of liquidity sources are “participating” in the auction together with private market makers and arbitrageurs.

Other use cases

Opium is open-sourced and permission-less protocol, meaning that everyone can place any ERC-20 tokens at the auction and get the best available execution at that moment. When placing tokens at the auction, one would need to specify starting (very high) price and min price after which the auction will stop.

item.title: Opium V2: your out-of-the-box derivative protocol
item.dc:creator: Riccardo Biosas
item.content:encoded:
DeFi and CeFi: a tale of two worlds

One of the many lenses through which we can assess the maturity of the current state of DeFi is by ranking the volume of its financial instruments and then compare the findings to their CeFi counterparts.

As other analysts have already pointed out, the most significant disparity between traditional financial markets and the cryptocurrency market lies in the difference between the size of the derivative market and market share of spot assets.

While, in the traditional financial markets, derivative volume dwarfs equities and other spot assets by a multiple greater than 30, in the cryptocurrency market options are only a relatively thin slice of the pie.

The DeFi ecosystem has been so far a retail market largely dominated by spot exchanges. In hindsight, it was a logical trajectory as the mechanics underlying the financial primitives of spot exchanges are inherently more easy to implement than the financial wizardry required to concoct a derivative market.

However, as the rate of institutional adoption keeps increasing, the DeFi instrument volume ratio will start to mirror CeFi: this means a potential growth for the DeFi derivative market that could be many orders of magnitude.

The bottlenecks that have prevented the growth of the DeFi derivative market can be summed up in two main categories: technical and demographics.

If it is in large part true that the cryptocurrency market first started and then flourished thanks to its strong, diverse grass-root retail user-base, it’s also true that the same user-base has increased their financial literacy over time. In what has been a collective learning experience, it is likely that many of its zealous users — a.k.a. the degens — have become traders and, similarly, developers have become financial engineers. At the same time, the rate of adoption among institutional investors — hedge funds, corporations adding crypto-assets to their balance sheets etc.- has consistently increased over the past year.

To further prove the case, the volume of Deribit and other centralized cryptocurrency options platforms has witnessed an exponential growth in 2021: still not as high as their CeFi counterparts, but much higher than decentralized derivative exchanges.

So if the appetite for options of both users and investors is finally there and outmatches the current supply of financial products, then the only remaining reason for the current bottleneck in the DeFi derivatives market must be technical.

And if the bottleneck to a large extent is technical, how can we solve it?

This is the question that we, in the Opium community, wanted to solve with the design of Opium V2 and the new pool products that will soon be released on top of it.

The design dilemmas of a derivative protocol

Two of the top factors that determine the success of a DeFi derivative protocol are liquidity and flexibility.

Liquidity is essential for traders to ensure that there’s a market where they can exchange their assets. Flexibility is essential for financial engineers to ensure that a protocol allows them to seamlessly encode the financial requirements of their products: in other words, flexibility can be regarded as a good developer experience (DX).

Some protocol architectures, however beautiful and efficient for a specific use-case, tend to over-engineer their foundational layers, which ends up imposing constraints down the road in the breadth of products and financial requirements that they can support natively. One of the side effects of that is that the developers building on top of such an architecture will face implementation obstacles which will decrease the reach of third-party integrations.

Especially in an ecosystem such as DeFi, rooted in open-source development and governed by network effects, a software is only as strong as it is its adoption rate in the developer community.

The Opium protocol v2 is meant to be asset-agnostic, both in terms of supported underlyings and in terms of oracles.

It is intentionally minimalist in its set of assumptions about what a financial product traded on it should look like.

As such, the Opium Protocol v2 acts as a trustless settlement layer with escrow functionalities. Any kind of sophisticated business logic (options strategies, vaults, peer-to-pool with different AMM models, different types of products -call/put options, CDS, interest rate swaps-) is something that can be easily supported atop the protocol, but it is not explicitly encoded in its core contracts.

The responsibility of the protocol layer should be only to mitigate counterparty risk in a trustless fashion and ensure the internal consistency of its balance-tracking operations and other primitives, without any further assumptions on who and what assets ought to be involved in its transactions.

What’s new with V2?

At its core, Opium V2 uses a factory pattern to mint ERC20 tokens — representing SHORT and LONG positions- upon the creation of a derivative. Their creation is delegated to a factory contract that uses the create2 opcode to deterministically calculate the deployment address of a position based on their derivative hash as a salt.

The derivative hash acts as a unique identifier across the protocol that distinguishes each and every financial product deployed on top of Opium v2. It partially borrows inspiration from the design of the Bloomberg tickers and ISIN, where the uniqueness of their identifiers provides a guarantee that a trader is dealing with the desired product.

Gas Optimizations

As bytes manipulation — let alone string manipulation- can be unforgivably costly in Solidity, some niceties that have been implemented in the factory contract to optimize its gas consumption include the implementation of the EIP 1167 standard (Minimal Proxy Contract).

More customization for synthetic authors

Alongside its derivative hash, Opium v2 allows synthetic authors to assign a custom name to their derivative product. It is a purely cosmetic feature which, unlike the derivative hash, does not provide any guarantee of uniqueness and should not be relied upon for any critical business logic. However, should a derivative author create a series of financial products featuring many different synthetics, the possibility of customizing their positions’ names would improve their recognition in third-party derivative explorers.

More efficiency for arbitrageurs

Some of the other user-facing features featured in Opium v2 include the ability to redeem market neutral positions for their originally allocated collateral. The ability to be able to easily swap market neutral positions should make the user-experience of arbitrageurs and other market makers more smooth. Furthermore, they will be able to trade fractions of their positions — both market neutral and not.

Gasless permits for position holders

The EIP-2612 has been implemented in the Opium position ERC20 contracts to decrease the costs associated with changing allowances and transfers in secondary markets.

A more decentralized governance system and flexible oracle design

Lastly, a more granular governance system has been implemented that favors decentralization and ensures a single-responsibility separation of roles. Alongside that, Opium V2 now supports an even more flexible oracle design since, as of the new release, it does not enforce the synthetic oracles to comply with a specific interface.

Introducing decentralized Know Your Cat (KYC) technology for unique non-transferable IDs

Introducing Cheshire

Opium Team presents Cheshire cat avatars. It is a unique NFT that can be used for verification, achievements, reputation, or access to special products. Your Opium avatar may be transferable, however, the recipient’s address must confirm that it belongs to the same person.

Your avatar is a smart, wonderful, mystical, and magical creature — the Cheshire cat. For now, Cheshire has the most important part of its body — the smile and later can be upgraded with colored fur, clothes, and more attributes that will give him different super-skills in the DeFi world.

We are ready for Metaverse! And you?

Cheshire cats are not part of Opium Protocol but can be used to identify or verify users and community members for various purposes. For example, a fully regulated company that builds on top of the protocol will have an opportunity to use Cheshire as an ID to provide basic/extra services.

With our community we believe that DeFi will grow substantially, therefore it will require solutions for verifications and differentiation of user roles. Cheshire will have a set of parameters and achievements that will allow to get unique services and features directly from smart contracts.

How to mint

Initial minting of Cheshire cats will start around the New Year date for those users of Opium.Finance who accepted and signed the Terms and Conditions of that platform before 25 December 2021 and has a basic verification level. From January 2022 more companies who develop on Opium Protocol may utilize this amazing “Know Your Cat” feature.

You can get your basic NFT on Opium.Finance if you used it before 25 December 2021. On behalf of Opium Community we wish you a Merry LfL and Happy New DeFi Year.

Next steps — think of more

Before Cheshire can travel to Metaverse it should acquire a few attributes, get fur and clothes, unique reputation, and look. Various projects and developers will be allowed to add genes to the Cheshire DNA, however, the main genes will always stay unique since minted. Based on the DNA records on-chain and off-chain logic can be verified and triggered.

There can be special liquidity pools created for users with needed verification (ready for verification, “halal” finance, closed communities, etc). item.title: Build a call option on Opium
item.dc:creator: Riccardo Biosas
item.content:encoded:
The Opium protocol is a universal protocol to create, settle and trade virtually all derivatives and financial instruments in a professional and trustless way. It allows anyone to build custom exchange-traded products on top of the EVM-Compatible blockchains. Once created, they can be traded freely via a network of relayers and will be priced according to supply and demand.

In our tutorial we will walk through the logic of a basic call option on ETH as an underlying.

If you are not familiar with the concept of call option, have a look at this introductory article.

You can find all the code in this tutorial on github. As our repository uses the hardhat’s forking feature to run our tests against the Opium Protocol’s Ethereum Mainnet contracts, we will need an Infura project ID — or any other node service provider of your choice, you name it. Set your Infura project id and mnemonic in a .env file with INFURA_API_KEY and MNEMONIC as the respective environment variables.

Next, let’s clone the repository and try to run the tests.

git clone git@github.com:RiccardoBiosas/opium-call-option-example.git
cd opium-call-option-example
yarn install
yarn test

Assuming everything has been set up correctly, all unit tests should pass with a green check mark. Congrats!

Code walk-through

At the core of each financial product built on top of the Opium Protocol there are two main components: the derivative recipe and the oracle recipe. The former is responsible for encoding the financial specifications of the product, whereas the latter is responsible for defining the data source that should be used to settle the product at expiry.

The structure of these two components need to adhere respectively to the IDerivativeLogic and IOracleId interfaces. In our example repository the contract implementing the IDerivativeLogic interface is OptionCallSyntheticIdMock and the contract implementing the IOracleId interface is the AdminOracleController.

However, the OptionController contract is where all the interactions with the Opium Protocol’s Core contract reside. The Opium Protocol’s Core contract is responsible for most of the financial logic processed by the Opium Protocol.

Before moving forward, bear in mind that all the code showcased here was written to illustrate the life-cycle of a basic option product on the Opium Protocol, so it goes without saying that it’s not meant to be run in a production environment!

Having said that, let’s start breaking down the OptionController chunk by chunk!

The OptionController inherits LibDerivative, a contract which defines the blueprint of a Derivative and getDerivativeHash — a function to return the footprint of an Opium’s financial product based on the hash of its packed parameters.

In the constructor, we pass the address of the Opium’s Registry contract. The Registry contract allows us to fetch and then store the addresses of all the Opium contracts that we need to implement our basic call option’s workflow. We’ve already introduced the Core contract, the other two contracts are the SyntheticAggregator and the TokenSpender. The SyntheticAggregator contract is responsible for caching and initializing a given financial product’s data, whereas the main responsibility of the TokenSpender contract is to manage the transfer of ERC20 tokens (i.e: at the moment of a derivative’s creation where an ERC20 token represents the product’s collateral or when a derivative is being settled and therefore the payout is being forwarded to the rightful party).

Then we set up our own derivative by calling the setDerivative function, which takes as an argument a LibDerivative.Derivative and stores it on the contract’s scope. Note that normally we wouldn’t need to do that, and that obviously in our example the owner could override the derivative variable in the middle of its life-cycle — but again, for the sake of breaking everything down step by step we will not concern ourselves with any practical design consideration.

Now that we’ve got our derivative, we are ready to mint its positions.

We call the create function. The OptionController’s create function is a wrapper around the Core’s create function. As an argument, it takes the _amount of derivatives (LONG/SHORT positions) that will be minted and the addresses of the buyer and the seller. Do note that in financial literature the buyer is associated with a LONG position and the seller is associated with a SHORT position.

The LONG/SHORT positions being minted are based upon the derivative that we have previously defined with the setDerivative function. In order for our create function call to be successful, the Core contract must be provided with the the appropriate margin. The required margin of our derivative is computed by the _computeMarginRequirement helper function, which adds up the long position’s and short position’s margins and multiplies them by the requested quantities.

And that’s it! We just minted our first positions.

Let’s now have a look at the callOptionWithDAICollateral tests.

opium-call-option-example/callOptionWithDAICollateral.ts at main · RiccardoBiosas/opium-call-option-example

First things first, here’s the derivative recipe of our ETH call option:

Here we specify the required margin, the maturity, the strike price, the address of the OracleId — our oracle recipe, the address of the token used as a margin and the address of the SyntheticId — our financial recipe.

In the tests workflow, the optionSeller account locks 400 DAI (derivative recipe’s margin * amount) in the Opium Protocol and receives an equal amount of LONG/SHORT ERC721O tokens. The seller is said to be market neutral until she exchanges her LONG positions with a buyer for 20 DAI.

Subsequently, now the seller holds only SHORT ERC721O tokens and the buyer holds only LONG ERC721O tokens.

The Opium Protocol supports European options. This means that any option created on top of the protocol can only be settled at expiry. As the expiry of our derivative is hardcoded to be 40 minutes in the future since its creation, in our tests we time-travel after the expiry so that our seller and buyer can exercise their positions.

Once again, for the sake of clarity we split the logic pertinent to the execution of the LONG/SHORT positions into two separate functions in the OptionController contract: respectively executeShort and executeLong.

Both functions are a wrapper around core.execute and they take the amount of positions to be exercised as an argument. Within their body, they calculate the hash of our derivative via LibDerivative.getDerivativeHash . Subsequently, they calculate the appropriate token id. For that purpose, we are using the LibPosition library which we attached to the bytes32 type. And now that we have computed on-chain all the necessary parameters, we can finally call core.execute !

Back to our callOptionWithDAICollateral tests, note that since both the seller and buyer accounts are interacting with the OpiumOptionController rather than directly interacting with the Opium Core contract, we need to enable the ‘third-party’ execution of the derivative by calling allowThirdParty. More generally, whenever the msg.sender is different from the EOA that holds a position, then calling allowThirdParty is necessary.

For a derivative to be settled, the data necessary to determine its outcome must be available (i.e: the current market price of the underlying against the strike price). In the Opium Protocol, the source of that data is the OracleAggregator. Normally — and ideally- the OracleAggregator would receive the required data from an on-chain oracle — such as Chainlink, UMA etc.-, but as the OracleAggregator was designed to be implementation-agnostic, in our example workflow we make use of AdminOracleController contract which receives off-chain data from its owner and then pushes it to the OracleAggregator. In our unit test we push a market price that is lower than the strike price, resulting in a favorable outcome for the seller of our ETH call option. The specifics of the payout of an Opium’s option are fully customizable and are defined in the getExecutionPayout of the contract implementing IDerivativeLogic.

In the case of our ETH call option, the seller received back the initial margin allocated to mint the LONG/SHORT positions. As the seller sold her LONG positions for 20 DAI, her profit amounts to 20 DAI. On the other hand, our buyer bought his LONG positions for 20 DAI, which corresponds to his net losses.

Vice versa, if the call option had expired in the money, the buyer’s payout would have amounted to the intrinsic value of the option unless the difference between the underlying’s market price and the strike price is greater than the allocated margin — in which case the buyer’s payout would be the entire option’s margin. As a result, the seller’s net loss would be 380DAI (margin * amount — paymentFromBuyer ) and the buyer would scoop up 380DAI as a profit!

Congrats, you built your first basic option call on top of the Opium Protocol!

Now that you got your feet wet, get in touch with the Opium community on the governance forum, the Opium DAO is eager to give grants to DeFi builders with interesting use-cases!

item.title: First Decentralised Protection for RealT “no-occupancy” event was launched on Opium Protocol
item.dc:creator: Opium Team
item.content:encoded:
Users of RealT platform can get decentralised protection

Why it is important

RealT.co is a progressive technology platform that offers investors the ability to purchase fractional real estate powered by blockchain. For around $50, you can purchase one token (or as many as you would like to invest) of a property. Investors are then paid a percentage of the tenant’s rent based on their investment in USDC through Ethereum or xDai network.

Opium, based on Ethereum, is a decentralized protocol, hosted through the Polygon network. One of the main use cases of Opium is protection (decentralised insurance).

Currently, all the properties offered on RealT.co are covered by the standard insurance to protect them from real estate disasters like fire and water damage. What is not insured, is the occupancy (monthly rent payment).

For example, in the event of a fire, it might take three months for repairs and renovations. The renovation expenses are covered by the property insurance; but if the tenant has to relocate, they do not pay rent during this time. This means rent will not be distributed for this property for those 3 months. The insurance offered through Opium Protocol will continue to distribute rental payments when the tenant doesn’t pay. Protection by Opium ensures RealT member’s cash flows.

How it works

I. Buyers

Buyer goes through several steps here.

  1. Choose a nominal to protect. The amount of rent you expect to receive from your RealT property and want to protect; may be higher or lower than the actual rent you receive now. But based on this nominal you, the premium that you pay will be calculated. In case of no occupancy (and no-rent), you will be compensated proportionally to the nominal.
  2. Transfer a premium to the decentralised smart contract and get a tokenised position.
  3. In case of “no-occupancy” during the protection period and lower rent, you will be automatically compensated with the difference from the smart contract. For example, you ensure $100 rent for a month. If there were no tenants for two weeks and RealT distributed only $50, you will automatically get $50 from the smart contract. In case of no tenants for the whole month, you will get $100 from the smart contract.
  4. It is essential to say that once “no-occupancy” occurred, sellers of protection can not unstake their funds until tenants are back again.
  5. Rental insurance by Opium smart contracts is available the first five days of each month when rent is expected. If rent is not paid by the seventh day of the month, Opium will cover the rent for the month portion and trigger a deposit into the investors wallet equaling the unpaid amount. For example, if a buyer is expecting $20 of rent every month, on the seventh, if the rent is not paid, then they will receive roughly $5, one weeks worth. The following week a similar calculation is made until the end of the month.

II. Sellers (stakers)

Sellers can stake in the decentralised pool if the expect full occupancy.

  1. By staking money into the smart contract pool, you take the risk of “no-occupancy”. According to a decentralised optimistic oracle, if there are no tenants (no-rent) in the building, your collateral will be used to compensate buyers of the protection automatically.
  2. Once “no-occupancy” occurred, sellers of protection can not unstake their funds until there are tenants again. They may lose all collateral in the situation that there are no tenants for a long time.
  3. You can unstake every first day of the month or transfer your stake (LP position) as a simple ERC-20 token. Your stake (LP position) is accumulating all the buyer premiums of the protection pool.
  4. The more stakers are in the pool, the more time of “no occupancy” it may cover and the less yield (APR) a staker receive. The pool’s maximum size is limited to full-year rent, so the corresponding minimum APR is 10%. If the pool size covers only six months of “no-tenants”, the APR will be 20%.
  5. So far, the maximum “no occupancy” with RealT properties was three months that makes the mathematics of this decentralised protection fascinating.

About Opium & RealT

Core contributors of both protocols were working significant time together to develop the prototype of DeFi protection. Traditional insurance for “no occupancy” is costly and may be challenging to structure legally in different countries. Still, at the same time, “no occupancy” is a transparent event that can be validated using one of the optimistic oracles (Gnosis SafeSnap, UMA, Opium).

With both communities’ participation, the first simple protection primitive was developed on top of the Opium Protocol. After user feedback, it can be improved to have a better user experience (automatic prolongations etc.) and even be an option that is included as a checkbox on the RealT platform.

It was decided during RealT bi-monthly Community Calls that protection would be available to all RealT users (subject to KYC and whitelist on-chain).
